t: a fixed sin offering. One that is always brought from an animal, unlike the "variable offering" (oleh veyored), which changes according to the person's financial means (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).
one who dissolves. One who crushes or melts it into a liquid.
it will have no permitted use as food. And this includes any other permitted use (compare Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:15).
and one who leaves. One who leaves it in place.
in his possession. In a place that belongs to him.

the prohibition of chametz and the prohibition of se'or in it, which leavens, are one. Therefore one transgresses both of these prohibitions not only with se'or, which is a sour dough of water and flour used to make other dough rise, but also with chametz (see its definition below 5:1).
so that he performs an act. To be liable to lashes one must perform an act, since one is not flogged for a prohibition that involves no act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
lashes for rebelliousness. Rabbinic lashes.
chametz over which Passover has passed. That was in the possession and ownership of a Jew during Passover (and see below chapter 4).
by rabbinic enactment. By enactment of the Sages.

they prohibited it even if he left it unintentionally or under duress, so that a person not leave chametz in his possession, etc.. Out of concern that he might come to leave it deliberately, they penalized even one who left it unintentionally or under duress.
whether of its own kind. For example, wheat that became leavened and was mixed with wheat that did not become leavened.
or not of its own kind. For example, wheat that became leavened and was mixed with barley or another kind.

it prohibits in any amount. Unlike other prohibitions that are nullified in a mixture by a ratio of sixty or by a majority, here, because of the severity of its prohibition, chametz is not nullified at all (for the reason in detail see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:9, 15:12).
if it was mixed, whether of its own kind or not of its own kind. Whether it was mixed during Passover or after it.
for they penalized and prohibited only chametz itself. When it exists by itself.
Babylonian kutach. A relish made of various things into which flour is mixed (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 3:1; Nedarim 6:3).
and Median beer. An intoxicating drink made from a soaking of wheat and barley (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim, ibid.), like our beer.
you shall not eat anything leavened. From this we learn the prohibition of anything in which chametz is mixed.

if he ate an olive-bulk of chametz within the mixture in the time it takes to eat three eggs' worth. The chametz within the mixture that he ate combines to the measure of an olive-bulk, and he ate it within the time required to eat bread of the size of three eggs (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:8).
but if the mixture does not contain an olive-bulk in the time it takes to eat three eggs' worth. And thus there is no substance of chametz in this mixture (see ibid. 15:3).
even though it is forbidden for him to eat. For it is forbidden to eat even a trace of chametz.
lashes for rebelliousness. Rabbinic lashes.
on the fourteenth day. Of Nisan.
from the beginning of the seventh hour of the day. The day is divided into twelve equal parts (seasonal hours), six before noon and six after noon, and the seventh hour begins at midday.
from oral tradition. From the tradition of the Sages.
you shall not eat chametz from the hour that is fit for slaughtering the Passover offering, etc.. See also below 2:1.
so that he not come near a Torah prohibition. To keep him far from a Torah prohibition.
a decree because of a cloudy day. When the sun is not visible, it is hard to tell the hours exactly.
therefore. Because the rabbinic prohibition of benefit begins only in the sixth hour.
we leave it in suspense. We leave it without a decision.
we neither eat nor burn. We do not eat because of the Sages' decree, and we do not burn because the prohibition at this hour is only by decree.
from oral tradition. From the tradition of the Sages.
that this "first" is the fourteenth day. Of Nisan, which is first and precedes the Festival of Matzot, and not the first day of the Festival of Matzot itself, which is the fifteenth.
you shall not slaughter the Passover offering while chametz is still extant. That chametz must not exist at the time the Passover offering is slaughtered (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:5).
the fourteenth day after midday. See ibid. 1:4.
in hiding places. In concealed places.
that one searches and nullifies. That after the search one nullifies the chametz (see below 3:7).
and they do not fix a session of study. Public study.
a scholar should not begin to read. Even when studying alone.
lest he be drawn on. In his study.
neither by moonlight nor by sunlight. Because their light is not sufficient for a thorough search in holes and hiding places.

nor by the light of a torch. Several candles burning together; because it has a large flame and might cause a fire, a person is afraid to bring it into holes and hiding places and will not search properly.
a portico. A roofed open area at the entrances of houses.
in the middle of the house. At mid-height of the wall, neither too high nor too low (see below 5:6).
between one person and another. In the shared wall between two tenants.
the projecting ledge. A structure attached to the outside wall of the house (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 1:4); because its roof is sloped, chametz cannot be placed on it.
and chicken coops. Chicken coops.
and storerooms. Warehouses.
from which he does not draw. That he does not take wine or oil from these storerooms during his meal.
and a house of large fish. Which are usually taken out before the meal, and one does not go in to take them out during the meal.
they do not require a search. Because ordinarily chametz is not brought into these places.
but storerooms of beer and storerooms of wine from which he draws. He brings beer and wine from them during his meal.
and the wax house. From which wax is brought during the meal to light the candles used for lighting.
and the wood house. Wood used as fuel for heating during the meal.
muries. A salty relish of fish brine in which bread is dipped.
the cellar. The wine storeroom.

the two outer rows, which are the top one and the one below it. The row next to the ceiling and the one beneath it, among the rows closest to the entrance door, since a person takes from these rows first.
a weasel. And the like.
for if we were to suspect from house to house. If we were to suspect that a weasel dragged chametz from one house to another.
piles. Heaps.

for anything fixed is like half and half. Although most of the piles are of matzah, we do not follow the majority here, because the minority (the pile of chametz) is fixed in its place and stands on its own; therefore it is significant and is not nullified by the majority, and the doubt becomes evenly balanced (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:11).

two piles, one chametz and one matzah, and two houses, one searched and one not searched, etc.. Since one house is not searched, we assume that the mouse that took the chametz went in there, and the mouse that took the matzah went into the searched house (see also Hilchot Terumot 13:14).

and likewise two searched houses and one pile of chametz, and a mouse came and took it, and it is not known which house it entered. Because for each house we can assume that it entered the other house.

or he knew that it entered one of them, and he entered after it and searched and found nothing, or he searched and found a loaf. And thus there is no concern of chametz either in this house or certainly in the other house.

for there is nothing fixed here. Unlike the previous halachah, where we are unsure whether chametz or matzah entered a particular house, in these cases the doubt is whether anything at all entered a particular house, and so the doubt is not fixed in the house itself (Maggid Mishneh; and see Kesef Mishneh for a different version of this halachah).
he put the chametz in one corner and found it in another corner. And it is possible that the chametz he put down was lost, and the chametz he found is other chametz.
a charmer. A person who knows how to handle snakes.
in the heavens of a beam. On top of a beam in the ceiling of the house.
a lump of leaven. A clump of sour dough.
that he designated for sitting. That he set aside to sit on, not for eating.
if he smeared its surface with clay. He covered it with a layer of clay, thereby ending its status as leaven.
the kneading trough. A large vessel in which dough is kneaded.

if it was made to strengthen the cracks of the trough or to plug a hole in it, it is nullified by being a minimal amount. For ordinarily a person treats it as part of the vessel, since he does not want to remove it from its place.

and if not, he must remove it. Even if there is not an olive-bulk of chametz in one place, because when it is not for the sake of the trough, there is a concern that he will take it and add it to another piece and reach an olive-bulk of chametz (see the next halachah).
if there were two half-olive-bulks in two places. In the cracks of the trough.
and a thread of dough between them. Connecting them.

anything such that if the thread were lifted they would be lifted with it. If the thread of dough is strong enough that when it is lifted it pulls up with it the two pieces of dough attached to it, it joins the two pieces to make an olive-bulk, and he must remove it.
because sometimes he gathers them. When cleaning his house he collects them together, and an olive-bulk is found in one place.
since these half-olive-bulks are stuck to the walls or the beams or the floors. And there is no concern that he will gather them into one place.
without specification. Without explicitly saying whether it was searched or not.
if before he handed over the key. The landlord to the tenant.
the fourteenth arrived. The night of the fourteenth.
one who rents out a house on the presumption that it is searched. That he rented it out after the fourteenth had arrived, as stated above in the previous halachah.
and it is not a mistaken purchase... for he is performing a mitzvah. A person is content to perform a mitzvah himself, even at his own expense.
within thirty days. Before the night of the fourteenth of Nisan.

he is obligated to search. For thirty days before the festival, preparation for it begins, like other laws connected with a festival that begin thirty days before it (see Hilchot Yom Tov 6:24, Hilchot Avel 11:6).
one who makes his house a storehouse. Turns his house into a warehouse.
if he intends to clear it out before Passover, he must search. There is a concern that he might clear it out on the eve of Passover at twilight, find chametz, and have no time to remove it.
when a person searches. The search for chametz.
the corners. The corners.
until the beginning of the sixth hour. When the Sages prohibited chametz both for eating and for benefit (see above 1:9).
until four hours. For from the fifth hour onward chametz is not eaten (see above 1:9).
in a known corner. In a designated corner.
and is careful with it. That it not be scattered or lost.
and found it missing. For example, there were ten pieces and nine remained.
and to search again. To perform the search for chametz a second time (see above 2:12).
if the fourteenth falls on the Sabbath. And chametz cannot be searched for on the night of the fourteenth because it is the night of the Sabbath.
on the night of the eve of the Sabbath. On Thursday night, the night of the thirteenth.
and if any chametz remains on the Sabbath day after four hours. For this chametz cannot be removed on the Sabbath.
he nullifies it. In his heart, and recites the text of nullification (see the text below 3:7).
and covers it with a vessel. So that he not come to eat it.
until the end of the first festival day. For even on a festival it is impossible to remove chametz.
and he must burn it on the eve of the Sabbath. Because on the Sabbath he will not be able to eat all the loaves, and he must see to removing them before the Sabbath.

he must not mix the pure with the impure and burn. Because the time for burning the chametz has not yet arrived, he may not defile the pure terumah and burn it together with the impure (see Hilchot Terumot 12:1).
and the suspended. Terumah that is in doubt whether it is impure or pure.
at the time of removal. The sixth hour.
during the festival. During the days of Passover.
he searches after the festival. After the days of the festival have passed.
because it is prohibited for benefit. By rabbinic enactment (see above 1:4).
as we have explained. Above 2:5-6.

and if he searched after the festival, he does not recite a blessing. Because this search was not for the mitzvah of removing chametz, since the time for removal has passed, but only so that he not benefit from chametz over which Passover has passed, which is a rabbinic penalty (see above 1:4).

any chametz that remains in his possession and he does not see it. Even though he searched and must remove whatever he saw, it is possible that some chametz remained that he did not see, and he must nullify it.
he need not nullify. Because his nullification is of no effect.
for it is not in his possession, since it is already prohibited for benefit. Chametz, once prohibited, is not in a person's ownership, and therefore he cannot nullify it.

and from six hours onward he found chametz... he has transgressed "it shall not be seen and it shall not be found". That he transgresses these prohibitions from the beginning of the sixth hour. Some delete the words "and from six hours onward" and read "if he did not nullify before six and found chametz"; according to this reading, the finding of the chametz takes place during Passover, and Rambam's view is that he transgresses these prohibitions only from the start of the night of the fifteenth of Nisan (see the edition of Rabbi Y. Kafih).
for everyone keeps away from it. So that they not come to misuse sacred property (me'ilah) (below 4:2).
from the hand of a troop. An enemy army.
from the river. From drowning in a river.
from the fire. A conflagration.
he went out for his own needs. And not for a mitzvah or for rescue.
and how far must he return. For what quantity of chametz left in the house must he return to remove it.
one who left, etc.. After the time of removal.
a rolled dough. Water and flour mixed that has not yet leavened.
earth three handbreadths or more. At a height of three handbreadths or more.
it is as if removed. And he need not dig beneath the collapsed debris to take it out and remove it.
he gave it to a gentile. As a gift.
he need not remove. For one need not remove chametz that belongs to a gentile (below 4:1-2).
and if he burned it before the sixth. Before it became prohibited for benefit.
it is permitted to benefit from its charcoal during Passover. Since it ceased to be food before it became prohibited, it is not considered chametz (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 16:24).

that bread and that cooked dish are prohibited for benefit. For in preparing the bread or cooked dish he benefited from the heat of a prohibited chametz fire (see also ibid. 16:22, Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:13).
one might think that if he buried it or deposited it... he would not transgress. For he does not see the chametz.
but if it was far from his house, in a field or in another city, he does not transgress. For this chametz is not within his reach, and it does not fall under "it shall not be found."

but you may see that of others and that of the Most High. And you do not transgress "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found" even when this chametz is accessible to you and found in your possession.
a resident alien. A gentile who accepted upon himself the seven Noahide commandments and who may be permitted to settle in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7).
over whom the hand of Israel rules. And they can compel him to remove or destroy his chametz.
lest he come to benefit from it. To eat or benefit from it during Passover.
me'ilah. Forbidden benefit from the sanctified property of the altar or the Temple (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:1).
and it is permitted to eat from it after Passover. And it is not considered chametz over which Passover has passed, which the Sages prohibited (see above 1:4).
for it is in the gentile's possession. In the gentile's ownership.
a violent man. A violent and dangerous person.
the oppressor. This dangerous gentile.
that he pledged as security. Gave as collateral against a loan.
if he said to him. The Jew to the gentile.
it is in the gentile's possession. And it is considered the gentile's chametz during Passover.

provided that the time he set for him is before Passover. For example, he said to him, "If I have not brought you the money by the thirteenth of Nisan, acquire this chametz from now." In this case, if he did not pay his debt before Passover the chametz is acquired by the gentile and is considered his during Passover. But if the Jew set the repayment date after Passover, the acquisition does not take effect until after Passover, and during Passover the chametz was owned by the Jew.

and if he did not say to him "acquire it from now". Even if he set a time before Passover, and the Jew did not come to repay his debt until after Passover, since he did not say "acquire from now" the chametz was not acquired by the gentile, for a gentile does not acquire a pledge unless the Jew explicitly transferred it to him (see Hilchot Mechirah 11:6-7); it was therefore with him as a mere deposit and owned by the Jew during Passover (based on Responsa Birkat Avraham 22, cited in Yad Peshutah).

and the fifth hour arrived. When the chametz is still permitted for benefit; but from the sixth hour onward he cannot give or sell it, since it is already prohibited for benefit and is not considered his (see above 3:8).
and takes it back from him after Passover. During Passover the chametz is the gentile's, and it is not considered chametz over which Passover has passed (see above 1:4).
a Jew says to a gentile. On the fourteenth of Nisan, before the sixth hour.
while you are buying for a maneh, come and buy for two hundred. He tells him to buy more than he wants to buy, thereby hinting that after Passover he will buy the extra back from him.
perhaps I will need it and buy from you after Passover. It is permitted to hint to the gentile that he will buy this chametz back from him after Passover.
but he may not sell to him or give to him conditionally. Explicitly.
he transgresses "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found". For his sale is not valid.
a mixture of chametz. Something in which chametz is mixed.
muries and Babylonian kutach. Relishes made of various things with flour mixed into them.
and Median beer. An intoxicating drink made from a soaking of wheat and barley.
the tanners' trough. The tanners' bowl.
it is permitted to keep it. Because the flour stinks and spoils immediately because of the hides.
for it has spoiled and become foul. And is unfit for eating.
within three days he must remove it. Because the flour has not yet become foul and is still fit to eat.
the eye salve. An ointment for the eyes.
and the plaster and the poultice. Bandages with salve for wounds (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:13; Kelim 28:3).
and the theriac. A remedy for snake bites and the like.
that became moldy. That became moldy.
and a poultice. A food that is chewed and placed on wounds for healing (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 8:1).
in wheat starch. Starch.
papers that were glued with chametz. It is the practice of scribes to make glue for books from the flour dust on the millstones (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 3:1).
for the form of chametz does not remain. For the form and purpose of chametz is as food (see also above 2:15).
in boiling water. Which hastens leavening (unless extremely hot; see below 5:3).
for this is not leavening but spoilage. And the swelling is not considered a prohibited leavening process.
in fruit juice. Juice that comes out of fruit.
without any mention of water in the world. Without mixing any water into it at all.

it is permitted to eat. Some read in place of these words, "one is not liable to karet for it" (see Ma'aseh Rokeach citing R. Avraham son of the Rambam); according to this reading, if he left the dough until it rose, one may not eat from it, but one is not liable to karet for eating it (and even according to this reading, if no signs of leavening appeared in it, it is permitted to eat it initially, as below 5:4).
and olive oil. Olive oil.
these cause leavening. Of the dough, and one is liable to karet for eating it.
ripot. Grain that was cooked, dried and ground (bulgur).
such as levivot. Dough cooked in a pot.
provided that they split in the cooked dish. The splitting of the wheat is a sign of full leavening under Torah law (below 5:8).
one may not roast dough. That was kneaded with water and has not leavened. For roasting it in oil, which is fruit juice, together with the water it was kneaded with, will cause it to leaven.
but one may cook bread and roasted flour. Which after baking or roasting no longer leaven.
because it cooks immediately before it can leaven. Because the water is extremely hot (this process is called chalitah - see below 5:17).
in Shinar. Babylonia.
and throughout the West. The lands of North Africa.
a decree lest he not bring the water to a proper boil. And the flour will leaven.
in fruit juice. Without water (as above 5:2).
carmel that is singed in fire. Grain kernels that have not fully ripened, which are roasted in fire.
when new pots are treated. They used to cook flour and water in a new pot to strengthen it.
they mix. They stir.
soft. Soft.
over the mouth of the oven-stove on which loaves are baked. An earthenware vessel placed over the fire, to which dough is stuck; the air space between the vessel and the coals gives off heat.
wheat may be mixed with water to remove its bran. To remove their husk. Because wheat is harder than barley, they did not worry about its leavening.
and in the Land of the Deer. The Land of Israel.
a decree lest they delay. That they not hurry to grind them, and delay in the water, and they leaven.
the whole dish is prohibited, for the chametz was mixed into it. And chametz prohibits the whole dish in any amount (above 1:5).

and if they did not split, one removes them and burns them and eats the rest of the dish. Although softened barley, even if it did not split, is prohibited as above 5:6, this prohibition is only rabbinic and does not prohibit the dish in any amount.

and it is only by rabbinic enactment, because it says "and you shall guard the matzot," etc.. Because of this exposition the Sages prohibited wheat and barley that did not split, even though they are not full chametz, because they have some aspect of leavening (this is the explanation according to the division of the halachot found in the manuscripts, and not as in the printed editions, where the exposition was separated from the preceding law and attached to the next halachah).
therefore. Since the Sages prohibited grain that came into contact with water because it has an aspect of leavening (as explained in the previous paragraph).
so too it is forbidden to keep it. By rabbinic enactment, because of "it shall not be seen and it shall not be found" (above 1:2).
rather, he sells it to a Jew and informs him. That this grain came into contact with water and should be eaten before Passover.
a drip. Dripping water.
it does not come to leavening. Because the dripping does not allow it to leaven.
if it was delayed for the measure. The time it takes to walk the distance of a mil (below 5:13).
one does not knead a large dough on Passover, lest it leaven. Because with a large dough it is hard for a person to work all of it (see below 5:13), and there is a concern that it will leaven.
only the measure of challah. Explained in the next halachah.
in hot water. Water heated by fire.
nor in water heated by the sun. Water heated by the sun.
nor in water drawn on that day. Because water drawn during the day was heated by the sun; the concern in all of these is that warm water hastens the leavening of dough.
but in our water. Water over which a night has passed after it was drawn, so that it cooled.
a woman should not sit in the sun and knead. For the heat of the sun warms the dough and it leavens quickly.
nor under the sky on a cloudy day, even in a place where the sun does not shine. For the light of the sun is diffused by the clouds and is present in every corner and direction.
and she should not leave the dough and busy herself with something else. For if she stops working it, it may leaven (see the next halachah).

and if she was kneading and baking, she needs two vessels of water. Since she is baking, her hands are heated by the heat of the oven and she must cool them with water. If she cooled her hands in the same water with which she smooths the dough, the water would become warm and hasten the leavening of the dough.
with which she smooths. She spreads water over the surface of the dough before putting it in the oven.
like forty-three and a fifth eggs. For the measure of challah by weight see Hilchot Bikkurim 6:15.
like the body of a medium egg. The volume of a medium egg.
and if he lifted his hand and put it down. If he took his hands off the dough.
and likewise if its surface turned pale, like a person whose hair stood on end. The surface of the dough turned white, like a person whose face turns pale from sudden fright.

and one is not liable to karet for it. For it is not considered full chametz except when it makes a sound when struck, or when it has stayed for a mil (Mishnah Pesachim 3:5 and Commentary on the Mishnah there).
it makes a sound. When one strikes the dough with his hand, as above.
both are to be burned. Even if they did not stay for the time it takes to walk a mil, since the one that makes a sound has certainly leavened, we assume that the other has leavened too.
decorated biscuits. Bread on which shapes are drawn.
because the woman lingers over them. During the time of decorating them.
and even if they were shaped with a mold. They made the bread in a form with a shape, in which case the preparation does not take long.
and likewise the water used during kneading. For cooling the hands (as above 5:12).
the bran. The waste of the flour.
but one may scald bran for them with boiling water. For scalding in boiling water does not allow leavening (see above 5:3).
and feeds them immediately. In this way there is no concern that it will leaven.
as long as he does not delay in front of them for the time it takes to walk a mil. Which is the time for dough kneaded with water to leaven (above 5:13).
a woman should not soak bran that she carries in her hand to the bathhouse. To use for cleaning her skin.
but she may rub it on her dry skin. She rubs the bran while it is dry, even if her body is wet from the water she bathed in or is sweating from the bathhouse.
and he may put it on his wound. For healing.
because they cause leavening. For saliva causes them to leaven.
into the charoset. A mixture of fruit in vinegar or spices eaten on the Seder night in memory of the mortar (below 7:11); because of its sharpness it quickly causes the flour to leaven.
into the mustard, and if he put it in, it should be eaten immediately. Because mustard does not cause leavening as quickly as charoset.

and on the first day it is forbidden to knead and smooth except with water alone. The matzah of the mitzvah eaten on the first night (Maggid Mishneh, and see below 6:5). Some explained that there is a prohibition on kneading all of the first day, which is the fourteenth, out of concern that he will eat this matzah on the first night, which is the night of the fifteenth (Yad Peshutah, and see Orah VeSimchah, who explains similarly).

so that it be the bread of affliction. As it says, "seven days you shall eat matzot upon it, the bread of affliction" (Deuteronomy 16:3), and it is not the way of a poor person to eat dough kneaded with fruit juice (called "rich matzah").
vessels in which chametz was used cold, one may use for matzah cold. Since with cold use the vessel does not absorb (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 17:3).
because its leavening is severe. And the chametz is absorbed in the vessel even in cold use.
like a house of leaven. Like a vessel in which leaven is kept.
an earthenware stove-plate. An earthenware vessel placed on the fire, to which dough is stuck.
in a first vessel. A vessel that comes into direct contact with fire.
pots and pans. Types of pots.
and boils them in it. Through this boiling ("hag'alah") the vessel releases the chametz absorbed in it (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 17:4).
and afterward he rinses them. To complete the kashering of the vessel and its cleaning (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 11:8).
and likewise knives: he boils the blade and the handle in a first vessel. Because they come into direct contact with boiling chametz.
the handle. The handle of the knife.
in a second vessel. Into which he poured from a first vessel.

and pours boiling water over them. There is no need to boil them in a first vessel, because they absorbed chametz only through its being poured into them, and so they release the absorbed chametz in the same way.
smeared and coated with lead. Smoothed with a lead coating.
that he wants to boil. In order to kasher it for Passover use.

he surrounds it with a rim of clay, etc.. He sticks clay around the rim of the vessel on its outside all the way around, and the boiling water, which stays a short while on the clay rim, kashers the rim of the vessel and its sides, which absorbed chametz.
but on the rest of the festival. After this night.
millet. A kind of grain (not among the kinds prohibited on Passover).
in every place and at every time. Even outside the Land of Israel and even when the Temple does not stand.

and the Torah did not make this eating depend on the Passover offering; rather it is a mitzvah in its own right. And therefore it applies even when the Passover offering is not brought (unlike maror; see below 7:12).
if he swallowed matzah he has fulfilled his obligation; if he swallowed maror he has fulfilled his obligation. Swallowing counts as eating.
for maror is secondary to matzah. Because nowadays maror is rabbinic while matzah is Torah law (Orah VeSimchah, and see below 8:8).
he wrapped them in fiber. Threads that grow on a tree and are not eaten.
he has not even fulfilled the obligation of matzah. Because the fiber separates between the matzah or maror and his mouth (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 3:5).
without intention. He did not intend it for the sake of the mitzvah.
an epileptic during his seizure. For example, a person with falling sickness (epilepsy) during his seizure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 7:5).
and afterward he recovered. On that same night.
from one of the five kinds. Wheat, spelt, barley, oats and rye (see above 5:1).

for it says "no chametz shall be eaten" and it says "you shall eat matzot". From this, chametz and matzah are linked to each other. [Note: some manuscripts read: "for it says 'you shall not eat chametz with it' and it says 'you shall eat matzot.'" According to this, the continuation of the first verse is "seven days you shall eat matzot upon it" (Deuteronomy 16:3), and so there is a link here between the chametz and the matzah mentioned in the two parts of the verse (and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 2:5). Likewise the second verse - "you shall eat matzot" - begins with the words "you shall not eat anything leavened" (Exodus 12:20), and there too chametz and matzah are linked to each other.]
things that can come to leavening. That have the ability to leaven.
there is no matzah in them because there is no chametz in them. They do not leaven but only spoil (see above 5:1).
if it has the taste of grain. See also Hilchot Bikkurim 6:11.
dog dough. Dough kneaded with coarse wheat ingredients and intended for animals (Commentary on the Mishnah, Challah 1:8).
when the shepherds eat from it. It is considered to have been baked for them as well (see also Hilchot Yom Tov 1:14, Hilchot Bikkurim 6:8).
for this is not guarded for the sake of matzah. Because the purpose of its baking was not for human consumption (see below 6:9).

matzah kneaded in fruit juice, one fulfills his obligation with it on Passover. Although fruit juice without mixing in water does not leaven dough (as above 5:2), it is not necessary that the liquid kneaded with the matzah be able to cause it to leaven (unlike the grain from which the flour is made, as above 6:4).
because of the bread of affliction, as we have explained. Above 5:20.
not with bran bread. Made from the waste of the wheat that falls off before sifting.
and not with coarse-bran bread. Made from the waste that remains after sifting, from which it is not customary to make bread, and which is not considered bread.
but he may knead the flour with its coarse bran and its bran. When he did not sift the bran and coarse bran out of the flour (see also Hilchot Bikkurim 6:16).
and we do not say of it, "this is not the bread of affliction". Although it is not the way of the poor to eat such clean bread.
in a pan. A pot placed on the fire in which the matzah is baked.
baking in the ground. He dug a hole in the earth near the source of heat and baked the matzah in it.
that no threads of dough be drawn from it when it is broken. When he breaks it in two, for that is a sign it was not baked enough and is not considered bread.
with a soaked wafer. Matzah that was soaked in water after baking.
that did not dissolve. That did not melt and crumble in the water so that its taste was nullified (compare Hilchot Berachot 3:8).
tevel. Grain from which terumot and tithes have not been separated, which is forbidden to eat.
first tithe from which its terumah was not taken. That the Levite did not separate for the priest the tithe from the terumah given him by the Israelite; it is forbidden to eat before this separation.
anything over which one recites Grace after Meals, etc.. See Hilchot Berachot 1:19-20.
challah. A portion of dough set aside for the priests as terumah.
which is not fit for everyone. For it is forbidden for a non-priest (an Israelite) to eat challah and terumah.
second tithe. The tithe separated after the first tithe, eaten in Jerusalem by anyone.
because first fruits have no permitted use in all settlements. For they are eaten in Jerusalem only (Hilchot Bikkurim 3:3).
and second tithe may be redeemed and eaten anywhere. See Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1-2.

loaves of thanksgiving offering and wafers of a nazirite. Loaves and wafers (matzot) that are brought with the thanksgiving offering and the nazirite's offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:17-18, 9:23).
that he made for himself. For his own offering.
matzah guarded for the matter of matzah alone. That is intended for human consumption.
but this is guarded for the matter of the sacrifice. For the loaves and wafers are meant to come together with the offering.
to sell in the market. To someone who needs them for his offering.
we soak a wafer for him in water. We soften the matzah for him by soaking it in water.
provided that it has not dissolved. For if it dissolved its taste is nullified, and one does not fulfill the obligation of eating matzah on the first night with it (above 6:6).
we do not conclude. We do not end the meal with another food.
he again eats an olive-bulk of matzah at the end. In memory of the Passover offering (see below 8:9).
so that it be recognizable that he eats it in the evening. So that it will be evident in the evening that he is eating it for the sake of the mitzvah.
lashes for rebelliousness. Rabbinic lashes.
a little before the afternoon prayer time. Toward evening, a little more than two and a half hours before sunset (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 10:1).
with appetite. With appetite.

but on the eves of other festivals, he may eat until dark. But out of respect for the Sabbath and festival he should refrain from fixing a meal from the afternoon prayer time onward (see Hilchot Shabbat 30:4, Hilchot Yom Tov 6:16).

to tell of the miracles and wonders done for our ancestors in Egypt. In addition to the daily mitzvah of remembering the Exodus from Egypt (see Hilchot Kriyat Shema 1:3), there is a mitzvah to recount it on this night.
as it says, "Remember this day on which you went out from Egypt," as it says, "Remember the Sabbath day". And there it was explained that this remembering is in words (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:1).

"because of this"... at a time when matzah and maror are laid before you. One who says "this" points to something specific, and from this we learn that it refers to a night when these things are placed before us.
even though he has no son. He is obligated to recount the Exodus on this night, although the commandment says, "you shall tell your son."
even great sages. Who know and are familiar with the story in its details.
even if they did not ask. Although some verses in the Torah mention that the story of the Exodus was told to children in answer to their question (Exodus 13:14, Deuteronomy 6:20).
according to the understanding of the son. His intellectual capacity.

so that the children will see and ask. Although the father is commanded to tell them even if they were not moved to ask on their own, it is a preferred way of fulfilling the mitzvah to tell the story by way of question and answer.
roasted grains. Roasted wheat.
and they remove the table from before them. They remove from before the reader of the Haggadah the table on which the food is placed (see below 8:1-2).
and likewise he begins with the disgrace, informing that we were slaves to Pharaoh. This is an additional disgrace with which he begins, and he ends with praise of the redemption from Egypt.
provided that he expounds "An Aramean sought to destroy my father". For this begins the account of Israel's descent to Egypt (see below the text of the Haggadah).

until he finishes the entire passage. Which describes the descent to Egypt and the slavery there, and the exodus from Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:5-8; the one who brings first fruits also recites this passage - see Hilchot Bikkurim 3:10).
who did not say these three things. And explain their meaning.
and all these matters are called Haggadah. From the beginning of the text of "Mah Nishtanah" mentioned above in halachah 3.
to show himself, etc.. To perform acts that demonstrate his going out from Egypt to freedom, as explained in the next halachah.
and he reclines in the manner of free people. Lying and leaning on the side.
they must not give him less. The charity collectors who give him his festival needs.
even the poorest in Israel does not eat until he reclines. Although because of his poverty he does not recline all year round, on this night he must recline.
a woman need not recline. Because the reason she does not recline all year is not poverty or servitude but her nature or modesty, she need not recline even on this night (cited in Orah VeSimchah).
and if she is a woman of importance she must recline. Because she is accustomed to reclining all year, she must recline on this night too.
and a son beside his father. Although ordinarily it is not respectful to the father for his son to recline before him, a father generally forgoes this honor toward his son.
but a student in front of his teacher does not recline. He is not permitted to recline, out of respect for his teacher.
and reclining to the right. Leaning the body on the right side.
he must mix them. With water.
according to the wine and according to the mind of the drinker. According to the strength of the wine and the habit of the drinker, it should be mixed with water.
and in each of the four he must not have less than a revi'it of undiluted wine. In each cup there must be at least a quarter of undiluted wine (to keep a ratio no greater than one to four).
and he has not fulfilled the obligation of freedom. Because this drinking is not pleasant and is not the way of freedom.
and he has not fulfilled the obligation of the four cups. Because he did not drink each one separately.
he recites a blessing over it by itself. Borei pri hagafen.
and recites over it the blessing of song. The blessing Yehalelukha (below 8:10; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 10:7).
and between these cups. Between the first and second, and between the second and third.
if he wishes to drink. Wine.

between the third and fourth he does not drink. Lest he become drunk and fall asleep and not recite Hallel. But the wine he drinks during the meal does not intoxicate (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 10:7).
a rabbinic mitzvah. By enactment of the Sages, and one does not recite a blessing over it (see Commentary on the Mishnah 10:3).
dried figs. Dried figs.
and they pound them. They crush them.
and they bring it to the table on the night of Passover. To dip the vegetable in it (below 8:2, 8:8).
that it is one positive commandment to eat the meat of the Passover offering with matzah and maror. See also Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:1-2.
chazeret. Lettuce.
and ulshin. This plant is called "hindiba" in Arabic (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 2:6). Some identify it with cultivated chicory, and some with garden maror.
and tamcha. This plant is called "saris" in Arabic (ibid.). Some identify it with common bitter lettuce, and some with the root of garden horseradish.
and charchavina. In Arabic "qarsana" (ibid.). Some identify it with the plant eryngo (sea holly).
and maror. A kind of wild lettuce that is very bitter (ibid.).
in their stalk. In their root.

he boiled them. He cooked them lightly in water without spices (note of Rabbi Y. Kafih to Commentary on the Mishnah, Berachot 6:8; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that "shaluk" means cooked a lot (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and elsewhere; and see Meiri there, who says the word is explained both ways - all depending on context).
he pickled them. He soaked them in a liquid for a long time.
the sanctification of the day. "Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons" (see the text, Hilchot Shabbat 29:19).
and the season. The blessing Shehecheyanu.

and afterward he recites the blessing on washing hands and washes his hands. For eating the vegetable dipped in charoset, because they enacted washing the hands before eating any food that is dipped in a liquid (see Hilchot Berachot 6:1-2).
and they bring a set table. In their day small tables were set before each person, and they would place these things on the table in front of the reader of the Haggadah (see below halachah 2).

and the meat of the chagigah of the fourteenth. A peace offering that was brought together with the Passover offering so that the Passover offering would be eaten when full (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:3, 10:12-13).
and nowadays. When the Temple does not stand, and so there is no meat of the Passover offering or the chagigah offering.
and eats an olive-bulk. Of the vegetable.
they remove the table from before the reader of the Haggadah alone. For only on his table is the food placed. They do this to arouse the children to ask (above 7:3).
the reader of the Haggadah. Who would read the Haggadah before those reclining, while the rest listen.
and the reader says. Although the son already asked when he saw the change, the reader recites the full text of "Mah Nishtanah" (see Yad Peshutah and Orah VeSimchah).
and this night, twice. For we dip the vegetable in charoset (above halachah 2) and the matzah and maror wrapped together (below halachah 6).
boiled. Lightly cooked in water without spices.
and this night, all of it roasted. For the Passover offering was eaten roasted only (Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:4).
and he begins with the disgrace, etc.. As explained above 7:4.
and he says, "This Passover offering that we eat, etc.". See also above 7:5.
two wafers. Two matzot.
he divides one of them. He breaks it in two.
over two loaves. Whole ones.
like other festivals. On which there is a mitzvah to break bread over two loaves (Hilchot Shabbat 30:9).
what is the way of a poor person? With a slice. For he buys or receives a slice and not a whole loaf.

nowadays, when there is no offering. And eating maror is a mitzvah by rabbinic enactment (above 7:12), unlike eating matzah, which is a Torah mitzvah even nowadays. Therefore matzah and maror are not eaten together.
and he should not leave it soaking in the charoset. Rather, he dips it and takes it out.
and this is a rabbinic mitzvah. Eating maror when the Temple does not stand (see above 7:12).
even an olive-bulk. At the very least.
and nowadays he eats an olive-bulk of matzah. In memory of the Passover offering, which was eaten after the chagigah peace offerings (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:3).
and afterward he washes his hands. The washing of hands after the meal (see Hilchot Berachot 6:1).
and he may finish Hallel wherever he wishes. Unlike the rest of the Seder, which must be conducted specifically in the place of the meal (see below halachah 14).
a place where they were accustomed to eat. When the Temple does not stand.
roasted. Roasted meat.
a decree lest they say it is the meat of the Passover offering. For the Passover offering is eaten only roasted, and he would appear to be eating sacred food outside, as follows.
and everywhere it is forbidden to eat a whole roasted lamb as one. For it closely resembles the Passover offering, in which the lamb is roasted whole (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:10).
it is permitted in a place where they are accustomed. Since these things are forbidden in the Passover offering, there is no concern that people will say it is the meat of the Passover offering.
he recites Kiddush over bread as he does on the Sabbath. See Hilchot Shabbat 29:9.
one who has no vegetable but only maror. And has no other vegetable to dip in charoset (see above halachah 2).
and eats again from the maror without a blessing. For he already recited "on the eating of maror" earlier.
one who has no guarded matzah. Baked for the purpose of eating, and only with it does one fulfill the obligation of eating matzah (see above 6:9).

he recites the blessing on eating matzah and eats an olive-bulk. And with this matzah he fulfills both the obligation of eating matzah and the obligation of eating the matzah eaten in memory of the Passover offering.

he does not eat again. Because he put it out of his mind in his sleep, and if he were to eat now, it would be as if he ate the Passover offering in two different places (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 9:1), and just as that is forbidden with the Passover offering, so too in the eating of matzah, which is in memory of the Passover offering.
they eat again. Since some of them remained awake, it is not considered putting it out of mind and a change of place for those who slept.
if they all dozed off, they may eat. Since they did not fall fully asleep but only dozed, it is not considered putting it out of mind and a change of place.

text of the Haggadah. The text of the Haggadah here includes the account of the Exodus, whose elements Rambam detailed in the previous chapters (see above 7:3-6, 8:2-5). Apart from slight changes, this text is identical to the Haggadah text found today, except for a few passages found in the Haggadot we have after the listing of the plagues, which deal with the number of plagues that struck the Egyptians - "Rabbi Yose the Galilean says: How do you know that the Egyptians were struck..." - and afterward the hymn "How many levels of kindness has the Omnipresent bestowed upon us" (see Seder Rav Amram Gaon, Siddur Rav Saadia Gaon, Machzor Vitry and others). Some wrote that Rambam did not include these passages here because they were not widespread in all countries and reciting them is not essential, but his own custom was to recite them (Ma'aseh Rokeach, citing R. Avraham son of the Rambam). It should be noted that today the word "Haggadah" means the Passover Haggadah including the whole Seder service. Note: the heading "text of the Haggadah" does not appear in the manuscripts and was added here for ease of reference.
